item.title: Intrusive Thoughts: Clarifying the Confusion
item.description:
OCD

Intrusive Thoughts: Clarifying the Confusion

Intrusive thoughts and unwanted intrusive thoughts can have many meanings.

Posted August 29, 2026

Key points
  • Depending on emotional and pathological context, intrusive thoughts can represent vastly different phenomena.
  • Unwanted intrusive thoughts in OCD do not cause people to commit acts of violence.
  • Unwanted intrusive thoughts in OCD do not indicate poor impulse control.
Source: Created with Gemini

In conversation, print, and social media, people have been using the terms "intrusive thoughts" and "unwanted intrusive thoughts" to refer to a wide range of thoughts, feelings, and images that enter our heads. It's important to make the distinction between the various types of intrusive thoughts. Depending on the emotional and pathological context, they can represent vastly different phenomena.

Many intrusive thoughts are benign, and some are pleasant and desired—for instance, falling in love, or a burst of creativity while composing a song.

Intrusive thoughts can include everything from funny, bizarre passing thoughts that make great stand-up comedy to a range of unwanted intrusive thoughts. These include command hallucinations that can occur in psychotic states, depressive ruminations, and any unwanted “self-talk” (including rumination). People may also use the term to refer to the content of trauma flashbacks that intrude into ongoing experience.

These intrusive thoughts, whether unwanted or not, are very different from the unwanted intrusive thoughts that characterize some types of OCD. We have noted press reports suggesting that Lindsay Clancy, currently on trial for murder of her children, must have OCD because her actions were driven by what she referred to as intrusive thoughts. But there is no report of Clancy ever having been diagnosed with OCD. She may have had terrible intrusive thoughts, but she was likely in a postpartum psychotic state, which was seemingly not adequately diagnosed or treated.

This case and others involving intrusive, disturbing, or unwelcome thoughts must be evaluated in the context in which they occur.

Who Commits Violent Acts?

Violence is characteristic of people with poor impulse control, people in the midst of psychosis, and people with actual malevolent intent such as psychopaths or antisocial criminals.

Diagnoses consistent with loss of impulse control may include intense psychotic states, bipolar mania, flagrant paranoia, or dissociated states secondary to extreme trauma. Still, violent acts driven by mental illness are rare, even in psychosis, and most violent acts, whether impulsive or intentional, are not caused by mentally ill people.

OCD is a disorder of overcontrol. It does not involve impulsive explosions of violence or harm.

Passing Intrusive Thoughts and Unwanted Intrusive Thoughts in OCD

Everyone has the former. “Normal” (passing) intrusive thoughts may not even be remembered. However, the unwanted intrusive thoughts of OCD can be torturous, persistent, and shameful, and can escalate in frequency and intensity. They are maintained by the paradoxical effort of trying to banish them from your mind, a phenomenon sometimes called the ironic effect.1

Some facts about unwanted intrusive thoughts in OCD:

  • They do not cause people to commit acts of violence. Passing intrusive thoughts are meaningless—often just associations, seemingly random, and frequently experienced as “out of the blue.” True unwanted intrusive thoughts in the context of OCD are the opposite of intent and contrary to one’s values and nature. This is why they are resisted. Unwanted intrusive thoughts are accompanied by images, feelings, sensations, and emotions. Just as in a nightmare, imagination can create an experience that is intensely vivid but still not reality.
  • Stuck unwanted repeating intrusive thoughts in OCD are not random: They mean the opposite of what they seem to mean. They get stuck because of one’s entanglement with them. This entanglement happens because they are so personally offensive, disgusting, or shocking, and the urge to resist them, argue with them, or struggle against them is so powerful. In fact, they do not need to be resisted, despite how they feel. They are just thoughts, feelings, images, or sensations. Nothing more.
  • Unwanted intrusive thoughts are the building blocks of obsessions. They are identified not by their content, but by how they feel and how they act. They repeat, they spread, and they intensify. They provoke imagined narratives of catastrophe or misery. They “feel” relevant, true, and important even though they are not. They may feel like urges, but they are not.
  • They do not indicate poor impulse control. It is overcontrol rather than undercontrol that feeds obsessions. Trying to control thoughts is a hopeless project that leads to a rabbit hole of increasing thoughts and anxiety. Elevated levels of anxiety come with emotional and perceptual distortions that give the thought the illusion of an urge or an intent that must be resisted.
  • They do not represent impulses, “repressed” desires, or unconscious wishes. Once again, they are the paradoxical result of trying to control thoughts that feel unacceptable.

OCD is a disorder of doubting. Frequently, one may “know” that the content of the intrusion is nonsense but may also experience obsessional doubt and feel the need to seek reassurance or checking (i.e., “Am I 'sure' that this is OCD and not psychosis?”). So even the most remote possibility is haunting.

Casual use of the term “intrusive thoughts” by people who are referring to hallucinations, depressive ruminations, intentional violent fantasy, or other completely different phenomena can cause so much unnecessary pain and suffering. It reignites doubts in people with genuinely harmless OCD thoughts.

item.title: We Expect Women to Do Invisible Work, Then Watch Them Fall
item.description:
Emotional Labor

We Expect Women to Do Invisible Work, Then Watch Them Fall

How invisible family labor burdens mothers and follows women into daughterhood.

Posted August 29, 2026

Key points
  • Women's family labor often goes unnoticed until they stop doing it, then everyone sees the gap.
  • "Daughtering"—the relational work daughters do—is as invisible and effortful as motherhood's labor.
  • A bold boundary can strengthen a relationship; disruption is often evidence of years of unseen effort.
  • We judge women in the spotlight by their breaking point, rarely by the years they held it together.

When women do invisible family labor well, it can look like they aren't doing anything at all. The appointment gets made. Someone notices the child needs new shoes. The birthday card arrives. Grandma gets called. The family shows up for Thanksgiving. Someone remembers the medication, senses the tension, checks on the struggling sibling, and knows which relationship needs tending.

Life just appears to happen. Until the woman making it happen stops. Then everyone notices.

The Work We Don't See

One of the first pieces that made this visible to me wasn't a psychology study. It was an essay by anthropologist Micaela di Leonardo, "The Female World of Cards and Holidays," about the unpaid kinship work women do to keep families connected—cards, calls, gifts, the maintenance of family as a social fact rather than just a biological one.

I remember reading it and thinking about my own photo shoots. Not just one, but many. My little family. My in-laws on both sides. My kids' school pictures. Milestones that felt too important to skip. Each one meant scheduling, showing up, paying for it, choosing the images, ordering prints, framing some, and mailing others out as cards. Add it up over a year, and it's not an afternoon's worth of work. It's days.

Nobody in my family could have told you that. I couldn't have told you that before I started counting. It's one of the things that makes a family feel like a family. And it's also just work, the kind that doesn't show up on anyone's list of things I did that week, and rarely gets recognized as commensurate with what it actually costs.

A 2026 study by Michelle Grocke-Dewey and Nicole Wanago asked mothers to identify the invisible work involved in raising children. Collectively, they identified 124 different tasks—not just doing things, but remembering, anticipating, monitoring, planning, and worrying. Other recent research has linked mothers' emotional and cognitive labor with greater perceived stress and poorer occupational balance.

Successful invisible labor tends to erase its own evidence. We notice the appointment that wasn't made more readily than the dozens that were. Competence disappears into everyday life. Failure becomes visible.

And Sometimes We Watch the Fall

The current Lindsay Clancy trial is an extreme and horrific example, and the deaths of her three children should never be reduced to a story about ordinary maternal overload. Her criminal responsibility is a specific legal question involving competing claims about her mental state (as I'm writing this post, the verdict has not yet come out). But the public conversation surrounding the case is revealing. Women are talking about maternal mental health, exhaustion, responsibility, and what happens when someone who is expected to care for everyone else is profoundly unwell herself. And what about the other people in the household who should help care for the woman who is caring for everybody else?

Maybe that conversation feels familiar because women already understand the underlying rule: You can carry an enormous amount without anyone noticing, but everyone notices when you drop it. And this pattern doesn't begin or end with motherhood.

Invisible Labor Begins Earlier, in Adult Daughterhood

We talk frequently about the invisible labor of mothers. We talk much less about the invisible labor of daughters. I study a form of family labor I call daughtering: the work women do to maintain relationships and contribute to their families from the role of daughter. My research has found daughtering to be active, effortful, and largely hidden from societal notice. In more recent research, my colleagues and I analyzed responses from 1,444 women describing what they do well as daughters. They described showing up, listening, remembering, connecting, supporting, enduring. Generally, daughters are making other people feel that they matter. Or, in another way of putting it: work. But we don't usually call it that. They're just good daughters.

Until a Daughter Stops

This makes the current conversation about adult-child estrangement particularly interesting. Online, some parents describe their estranged adult children as selfish, ungrateful, entitled, or too sensitive. Sometimes parents take the grievance public, telling an online audience about the child who stopped calling, stopped visiting, withheld access to grandchildren, or walked away.

And certainly, parents can be deeply hurt by estrangement. Adult children can behave badly. The existence of estrangement alone tells us very little about who was "right." But notice what becomes visible: She left. What remains invisible is everything before that.

One woman I interviewed described years of her mother bringing up the daughter's old boyfriend. She always spoke fondly, always "just reminiscing," always landing, to the daughter, as a quiet commentary on the family she'd since built with someone else. She'd asked her mom to stop. Her mom laughed it off.

Then one afternoon, browsing a TJ Maxx together, her mother tried to slide in yet another update about the old boyfriend, something she'd seen on Facebook. The daughter, now married with a baby in the stroller beside her, said: I'm taking a time-out from you. The baby and I are going next door, and we won't be ready to get back together until you're ready to move forward in a new way.

It worked. Her mother was stunned...and then she recalibrated. They finished the afternoon together. It worked because the daughter was actually willing to walk out of the store, or go home for the day, if that's what it took. And it worked because her mother, once she understood her daughter was serious, was able to absorb the point and change course instead of digging in.

Most mothers and daughters, in my research, want exactly this: to love each other well, even when it takes a bold or uncomfortable act to get the relationship back on track. Only a minority of mothers can't make that shift, and it's in those relationships that the deeper, longer-lasting disconnection tends to take root.

A woman cannot single-handedly create a healthy relationship. Yet women are routinely expected to maintain them, including, it turns out, the moment when maintaining them means briefly, deliberately walking away.

Make the Invisible Visible

Before asking, Why isn't she doing more? of a woman, try asking, What has she been doing that I haven't noticed?

  • Name the work. Notice who remembers, anticipates, checks in, worries, organizes, smooths conflict, and maintains relationships (not just who completes visible tasks).
  • Appreciate it before it disappears. Don't wait until she stops calling, organizing, remembering, or accommodating to realize how much her effort contributed.
  • Make the relationship reciprocal. Instead of asking women to get better at carrying invisible labor, ask what other people can carry (and what burdens can simply be put down).

Sometimes putting something down will be uncomfortable. It might look like leaving TJ Maxx with the baby. It might mean saying no to a Thanksgiving get-together across the country. It might mean refusing to laugh off the comment one more time. From the outside, that moment can look like the disruption; but the disruption may be the first visible evidence of years of invisible work.

If we only recognize women's labor once they stop performing it, we haven't really learned to see it at all.

item.title: Own It or Change It
item.description:
Self-Sabotage

Own It or Change It

Integrity is the distance between your mouth and your feet.

Posted August 29, 2026

Key points
  • For every behavior, there are secondary gains and losses.
  • If you keep repeating a behavior, your secondary gains are stronger than your secondary losses.
  • Even if you decide to change the behavior, you first have to own your secondary gains.
Source: Assael Romanelli

Co-authored by Galit Romanelli

I'm supervising Abe, an older couples therapist. In between cases, he shares that a few years back he had a gastric band put in. But he still finds himself eating chicken nuggets at midnight.

"I know it's not good for me," he says. "But I can't stop it. I'm addicted."

Because he's a therapist, I ask if he wants to work on this behavior systemically. He says sure.

Through a systems perspective, in every situation, dynamic, or behavior, you have secondary gains and losses for your action. Whether that is a dynamic in your relationship, a pattern in work, or eating chicken nuggets at midnight. The losses are the toll you pay for your actions. The secondary gains are what your actions give you.

Abe goes straight to the losses. "I'm unhealthy. I get heartburn. I'm disappointed in myself. I don't sleep. I have no willpower. I'm weak and pathetic. I'm an impostor. How can I preach to my clients to make changes when I have no control over myself? I feel like a hypocrite."

This is what we call violining: a long, loud solo about your losses while you cast yourself as a helpless victim who has no control and no agency.

Our working assumption is that no one is a victim. You always have a choice. So I tell Abe: "I'll give you the most generous interpretation, the one that hands you the most agency. The tax for that interpretation is that this narrative will also include more of your shadows that you are blind to."

Then I ask him about his secondary gains. What does he gain from eating nuggets at midnight? He freezes. "I have no gains."

I'm used to clients declaring that they have no gains and only losses. But look at their feet. They keep doing that action again and again, so obviously they have more gains than they mention.

I share this with Abe. He smiles and says: "OK, I'm ready to open my eyes. Let's do this."

The gains start pouring out. No one tells me what to do. Freedom. I earned it. My way to releasing pressure. It's a correction to my young self. Turns out that Abe was the fat kid for years, and was always told "don't eat this" and "don't eat that." Now he gets to eat as much as he wants and doesn't gain weight: a gastronomic Peter Pan. And finally, by seeing himself as addicted, he gets to hide. He's too weak. Nothing can be done.

He weighs the two sides. "The gains are stronger," he says.

He doesn't decide at that moment that he's going to stop eating nuggets. But something in him shifts. He stops seeing himself as a victim.

The Integrity Fork

What Abe is feeling is a lack of integrity. We define integrity as the distance between your mouth (what you say you'll do) and your feet (what you actually do). The smaller this distance, the more integrity you have. Abe's mouth is preaching control, while his feet are deep into the nuggets.

You can minimize the gap by changing your feet, or by changing your mouth. Changing your mouth means owning your current behavior without excusing or violining. Changing your feet means behavioral change. Both of those give you integrity.

That is the decision. We call it the integrity fork: Own it or change it.

Owning it means owning your secondary gains, which is the systemic way of owning your shadow. When you own them, the distance between your mouth and your feet shrinks. I’m choosing to continue this behavior. I have agency and choice. Compare that to feeling sorry for yourself, blaming someone else, or feeling helpless.

I invite Abe to take a deep breath. Can you own it out loud to yourself right now?

He owns his nugget-eating a couple of times. He starts laughing, and something in him releases. That is his first step toward minimizing the gap between his mouth and his feet: "I know it's not healthy for me, but for now I choose to keep eating chicken nuggets. It's my choice. I'm not blaming my wife, my kids, or my parents." A sentence like that blocks you from seeing yourself as a victim.

I also eat junk food at night sometimes. I know I shouldn't, and I do it anyway. The minimum I can do is own it.

The other option is you change it. You soften core beliefs, change your outlook, and start behaving differently. In systemic work, that is called second-order change. And that's hard because such change means giving up on some of your current gains. Even for Abe, with the heartburn and the sleepless nights, the gains are still stronger.

Now here's the kicker. Even if you choose to change it, you first have to own it. Both roads start in the same place. You still might feel bloated and guilty at midnight with your nuggets. But at least you’ll have some integrity.

The way to the integrity fork begins with mapping your integrity chart:

  1. Choose a behavior that you want to change.
  2. List your secondary losses. Let yourself violin. Get it all out.
  3. List your secondary gains. Stay until you hit at least 10, past the point where you swear there are none.
  4. Weigh them. Which side is heavier?
  5. Go through the gains one by one. For the ones you still need, ask if there's a healthier way to get them, a way that fits who you are today.
  6. Then you reach the integrity fork. Make the brave choice: to own it or change it.

When you do what you say and say what you do, you not only gain integrity but you experience deep positive liberty. Abe took the first step. Are you ready to own it or change it?

Galit Romanelli is a relationship coach, Ph.D. candidate, and co-creator of The Remarriage Roadmap.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.
